- `repn.highest.weight` (Error or typo; Wrong label: should be mf.siegel): As stated the line is not unique: in the irreducible representation Sym²(ℂ²) the lines of e₁² and e₁e₂ have the dominant weights (2, 0) and (1, 1), and a representation that is not rational, such as A ↦ |det A|, has no such tuple at all. The highest weight line is the one fixed by the upper unitriangular matrices; the replacement also adds the missing full stop. — Wrong label: Only Siegel modular form knowls link to it, for the weights of vector-valued forms. LeanBridge's blueprint files it under Modular forms › Siegel.
- `repn.irrep.gl` (Error or typo; Wrong label: should be mf.siegel): Only the rational (equivalently, holomorphic) irreducible representations correspond to highest weights: g ↦ |det g| is an irreducible finite-dimensional representation of GL(g, ℂ) with no highest weight. — Wrong label: Only Siegel modular form knowls link to it, for the weights of vector-valued forms. LeanBridge's blueprint files it under Modular forms › Siegel.
- `ring.dedekind_domain` (Error or typo): By ring.fractional_ideal the zero submodule is a fractional ideal (d·0 ⊆ D for every d ≠ 0), and 0·J = 0 ≠ D for every J, so only the non-zero fractional ideals are invertible.
- `shimcurve` (Error or typo): X(O;1)^big(ℂ) = O^×\ℋ^± fails for a general order: by strong approximation for the indefinite algebra B, B^×\B̂^×/Ô^× is ℤ̂^×/(±nrd(Ô^×)), which is nontrivial for example for O_p = ℤ_p + p M₂(ℤ_p) with p ≡ 1 mod 4 and p ∤ D, whose unit norms are the squares mod p, −1 being one of them. The identification needs the double coset to be trivial, which holds when nrd(Ô^×) = ℤ̂^×, for instance for O maximal or Eichler. Found in round ZR by a hand argument, not formalised.
- `shimcurve.decomposition` (Error or typo): The example newform is 13.2.e.a (as earlier in the same sentence).
- `shimcurve.disco` (Error or typo): Typo: the display ends with a full stop, but the sentence continues "where trd is the reduced trace".
- `shimcurve.eichler` (Error or typo): The knowl links the reduced discriminant (shimcurve.disco) but writes it disc(O), the notation shimcurve.disco uses for its square, and it never defines D. LeanBridge formalises the corrected reading (since round ZX2) and proves it when B is ramified at no prime (round AJ). Noted in round T8, not recorded until now.
- `shimcurve.label` (Typo): Spelling: "Gassman" for Gassmann, as in the next item and in modcurve.gassmann_class.
- `shimcurve.nrdmu` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): With the polarizations of shimcurve.polarized_order, nrd(μ)/discrd(O) need not be an integer: in B = (−1, 3 / ℚ), ramified exactly at 2 and 3, the order O = ℤ + ℤi + ℤj + ℤij has disc(O) = |det diag(2, −2, 6, 6)| = 144, so discrd(O) = 12, and μ = i is a polarization (μ² = −1 and iO ⊆ O) with nrd(μ)/discrd(O) = 1/12, or 1/6 in a maximal order containing O. Since nrd(μ) = −μ² is an integer, one fix is to take the square-free part of the integer nrd(μ)·discrd(O), which has the same square class as nrd(μ)/discrd(O); another is to strengthen the condition on μ so that discrd(O) divides nrd(μ). Which one matches the database's polarization degrees is for the editors to decide. Also: The replacement that the formalisation follows (PolarizedQuaternionOrder.polarizationDegree in LeanBridge): the polarization degree is the square-free part of the positive rational number nrd(mu)/discrd(O), which need not be an integer.
- `shimcurve.xd1` (Error or typo): shimcurve requires H to be an open compact subgroup of the enhanced group Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Ô^×, and {1} is not open: it has infinite index in the infinite profinite group Ô^×. The curve X(D;1) = X(O;1)^big of shimcurve is that of H = {1} ⋉ Ô^× = Ô^×, the inverse image of {1} ≤ Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ (O/O)^× at level 1.
- `shimcurve.xd1_star` (Error or typo): Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ {1} is finite, so it is not an open subgroup of the enhanced group Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Ô^×, as shimcurve requires of H. The curve X*(D;1), the quotient of X(D;1) by Aut_{±μ}(O), is that of the whole enhanced group H = Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Ô^×, the inverse image of Aut_{±μ}(O) = Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ (O/O)^× at level 1.
- `shimcurve.xdm1` (Error or typo): As in shimcurve.xd1, {1} is not open in the enhanced group Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Ô^× (it has infinite index in Ô^×), so it is not a valid H; the curve X(O;1)^big of the Eichler order O (X₀(D;M) in shimcurve) is that of H = {1} ⋉ Ô^× = Ô^×. Also, "that is Eichler of level M" qualifies the quaternion algebra instead of the order O; the first two replacements move it.
- `shimcurve.xdn` (Error or typo): The inverse image of (O/NO)^× under Ô^× → (O/NO)^× (or of {1} ⋉ (O/NO)^× in the enhanced group) is all of Ô^×, for every N, so X(D;N) would be X(D;1). The full level N curve has H = Γ(Ô, N) = ker(Ô^× → (O/NO)^×), the inverse image of the trivial subgroup, as in modcurve.xfull ("the inverse image of the trivial subgroup of GL₂(ℤ/Nℤ)").
- `shimcurve.xdn_star` (Error or typo): The inverse image of the whole group Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ (O/NO)^× is the whole enhanced group Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Ô^×, for every N, so X*(D;N) would be X*(D;1). The intended group is Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ Γ(Ô, N), with Γ(Ô, N) = ker(Ô^× → (O/NO)^×), the inverse image of Aut_{±μ}(O) ⋉ {1}. The knowl also uses N without introducing it, unlike shimcurve.xdn.
- `specialfunction.poincare` (Error or typo; Wrong label: should be cmf): The knowl asks for v(−I) = (−1)^k and for v trivial on G_s, which contradict each other for odd k when −I ∈ G (then −I ∈ G_s); the terms of the series are well defined exactly when v(h) = ε^k for every h ∈ G_s with γ_s⁻¹hγ_s = ε(1 b; 0 1), ε = ±1. Replacing γ_s by −γ_s (which also maps ∞ to s) multiplies every term by (−1)^k, so for odd k the series is determined only up to sign even when w | n, and replacing s by gs with g ∈ G multiplies it by the complex conjugate of v(g). Also: The Poincaré series span the cusp forms only for n ≥ 1: for n = 0 the series is the Eisenstein series at the cusp s, which is not a cusp form, and for n < 0 it grows exponentially at s. The cusp is written s elsewhere in the knowl (the round of 31 October review, confirmed). — Wrong label: A Poincaré series is a cusp form for a finite-index subgroup of SL(2, Z). LeanBridge's blueprint files it under Modular forms › Classical.
- `st_group.ambient` (Error or typo): Rechecked in round AI0; supersedes the entries of rounds ZR, ZX2 and AF, whose correct pairs it keeps. The dichotomy is false in the LMFDB's own data: mu(n) (weight 0, degree 1) with n >= 3 contains zeta_n, so it lies in no O(1), yet the page of mu(3) says it is contained in O(1) (round ZR). It holds for Sato-Tate groups of motives with rational coefficients; the others have ambient group U(d) (round AF). The round AF text said 'with n >= 3' also for SU(2) x mu(n) and N(U(1)) x mu(n), which is too narrow: these are generated with diag(1, zeta_n) (lmfdb/sato_tate_groups/main.py, lines 761, 815), so for n = 2 they contain diag(1, -1), of determinant -1, and lie in no USp(2); and in even weight none of them lies in O(2), not even for n = 1, since SU(2) has real dimension 3 and N(U(1)) has elements of order 4 outside its identity component, while the other component of O(2) consists of reflections. The branch leanbridge/st-ambient of the local LMFDB clone implements this rule in st_ambient. Inside GL_d(C), {A : AA^t = I} is the complex orthogonal group, which is not compact for d >= 2 (it contains (cosh t, i sinh t; -i sinh t, cosh t)), whereas the ambient group is the compact real orthogonal group (round ZX2). For the editors: st_ambient in lmfdb/sato_tate_groups/main.py (and its comment on mu(n) lying in O(1)) must follow the third change, and st_group.definition states the same dichotomy.
- `st_group.definition` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): Found in round ZR. "the Sato-Tate group is a compact subgroup of the orthogonal group" in even weight, but the database's 0.1.3 is mu(3), not a subgroup of O(1).
- `st_group.fourth_trace_moment` (Error or typo): In degree 2 the statement fails: the fourth trace moment of USp(2) = SU(2) is the Catalan number 2, and the proper subgroup N(U(1)) has fourth trace moment (6 + 0)/2 = 3 (6 on U(1), 0 on the other component, where the trace vanishes). For 2g ≥ 4 the value 3 for USp(2g) is right, and Larsen's alternative gives a larger value for every other infinite closed subgroup.
- `st_group.hodge_circle` (Error or typo; Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): Found in round ZR. The knowl's last paragraph calls the h^{p,q} Hodge numbers, and without the condition p + q = w the trivial homomorphism with h^{0,0} = d is a Hodge circle of any finite group. Also: The last sentence uses d both for the degree of G and for the dimension of X: a g-dimensional abelian variety has degree d = 2g and h^{1,0} = h^{0,1} = g, as Σh^{p,q} = d requires. The second condition does not say by which group the image of h is conjugated, and the readings differ: if G is generated by G⁰ = {diag(u, v, ū, v̄)} ⊆ USp(4) and an element acting on G⁰ by (u, v) ↦ (u, v̄), the G-conjugates of the image of h(u) = diag(u, u, ū, ū) generate G⁰ but its G⁰-conjugates do not. Under either reading the connected G = G⁰, the Sato-Tate group of a product of two non-isogenous CM elliptic curves over a field containing both CM fields, has no Hodge circle, since G⁰ is abelian and the image of h is a circle; requiring instead that the images of all homomorphisms h with the eigenvalue condition generate a dense subgroup of G⁰ would avoid this.
- `st_group.label` (Error or typo): n can have several digits, so it is the second entry of the GAP id [c, n], not its second digit: for the group 1.4.F.48.48a, [c, n] = [48, 48]. "we" is spurious.
- `st_group.moment_matrix` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): "reverse lexicographic order of exponent vectors" is ambiguous. For g ≥ 3, descending lexicographic order and the graded reverse lexicographic monomial order differ: (1,0,1) precedes (0,2,0) in the first and follows it in the second. Read as in the example of st_group.moment_simplex (comparing from the last coordinate), the readings differ already for g = 2, where χ_{e₂} would come before χ_{e₁}. The comparison should be spelled out. Found in round ZR. "The irreducible characters are ordered according to their highest weight": for the ambient group O(d) the highest weight does not determine the character, since the trivial character and the determinant have the same one. Restrict the sentence to odd weight, where the LMFDB has data, or state a convention for O(d) such as Weyl's partition with λ'₁ + λ'₂ ≤ d. Weyl's order is not a refinement of the highest-weight order of the identity component (O(2): 1, ρ₁, det, ρ₂, …), so the convention should be picked explicitly. LeanBridge proves Weyl's labelling is a bijection onto those partitions (round ZT). Also: The data settle the order (round ZR): exact moments computed from the Koike-Terada functions match the database's gps_st only in decreasing lexicographic order of (c₁,…,c_g), on all of 1.6.K.1.1a, on 1.6.B.1.1a (first two rows and diagonal) and on 1.4.{B,C,D,E,F}.1.1a; the deciding pair is e₁e₃ before e₂², with moments 7 and 10.
- `st_group.moment_simplex` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): Under the stated convention (e₁, …, e_g), E[a₂¹] has exponent vector (0,1) and E[a₁²] has (2,0); the example writes them in the order (e₂, e₁). With the correct vectors the listed order (0,1), (2,0) is ascending lexicographic, as the last paragraph says ("sorted lexicographically by exponent vector"), but not reverse lexicographic in its usual reading; the editors should make the two descriptions agree. They need not agree with st_group.moment_matrix: the data show the simplex is ascending lexicographic and the matrix decreasing lexicographic (round ZR). "Symmetry constraints will force the expectation to be zero otherwise" could also name the constraint, −I ∈ G. Also: Only the weighted degree Σ i·e_i has to be even: in odd weight −I ∈ G, and a_i(−g) = (−1)^i a_i(g) makes the moments of odd weighted degree vanish, but a moment with odd terms i·e_i need not vanish: E[a₁a₃] = 1 on USp(6), since Λ³(ℂ⁶) contains the standard representation. For g = 2 the two conditions agree, as 2e₂ is always even.
- `st_group.moments` (Error or typo; Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): Rechecked in round AI0 (the LMFDB scan of 2026-11-13); these pairs stand, the definition of a_i is now for the editors (next entry). 'can associated' and 'powers sums' are typos (round ZX2). Not every random variable has an integer moment sequence: on SU(2) the trace a_1 has E|a_1| = 8/(3 pi); the moments of the a_i, e_i and s_i, and of every polynomial in them with integer coefficients, are integers (multiplicities of the trivial representation). Binomial convolution of moment sequences computes the moments of sums of independent random variables, not of products (round AC). Also: As written, a_i is the coefficient of x^i, which the site does not use: on mu(2) = O(1) the coefficient of x in x - g is 1, with moments 1, 1, 1, ..., while the page shows 1, 0, 1, 0, .... The suggested text (round ZX2) makes a_i the coefficient of x^(d-i) in det(xI - g), so a_1 = -tr g, as st_group.trace_moments says (t = -a_1). But the pages of mu(n) are built with a_1 = +tr g (lmfdb/sato_tate_groups/main.py, mu_data, lines 718 and 721): for odd n they show E[a_1^n] = 1 and Pr[a_1 = 1] = 1/n, and mu(1) shows a_1 = 1 with probability 1, where the suggested text gives -1. The two conventions differ only for odd i in even weight, so only the mu(n) with n odd are affected. The editors must choose: keep this text and flip those two lines (E[a_1^m] = (-1)^m when n divides m, Pr[a_1 = -1] = 1/n), or define a_i = e_i, as st_group.moment_simplex does, and change st_group.trace_moments. st_group.probabilities defines a_i with the same words.
- `st_group.probabilities` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide); Typo): The same definition as in st_group.moments, and the same choice for the editors (see its entry of round AI0). As written, a_i is the coefficient of x^i, which the site does not use: for mu(2) = O(1) = {1, -1} the coefficient of x in x - g is 1, so that Pr[a_1 = 1] = 1, while the page shows Pr[a_1 = 1] = Pr[a_1 = -1] = 1/2 (lmfdb/sato_tate_groups/main.py, mu_data, line 721). The suggested text is that of st_group.moments, with a_1 = -tr g; it agrees with the pages except those of mu(n) with n odd, which show Pr[a_1 = 1] = 1/n where it gives Pr[a_1 = -1] = 1/n. The editors must either flip lines 718 and 721 of that file or define a_i = e_i, as st_group.moment_simplex does, and change st_group.trace_moments. Also: The book is Serre's 'Lectures on N_X(p)' (so spelled in lfunction.taxonomy); found while checking.
- `st_group.supgroups` (Error or typo (for the editors to decide)): Rechecked in round AI0; supersedes the round ZYa entry. 'No supergroups' contradicts the data: mu(2) is marked maximal although mu(4) contains it with index 2. ZYa's 'no rational supergroups' contradicts the site's code (lmfdb/sato_tate_groups/main.py) both ways: SU(2) and N(U(1)) are marked maximal (lines 766, 820) although SU(2) x mu(2) and N(U(1)) x mu(2) are rational (lines 748, 803) and list them as subgroups (lines 762, 816); and those two rational groups are marked non-maximal although their listed supergroups (the x mu(4), x mu(6), x mu(10) groups) are all irrational. The code's rule, in its comment at line 707, is to list only supergroups with the same ambient group; it fits every generated group once the ambient groups are right (st_group.ambient), except SU(2) and N(U(1)) in even weight, which lie only in U(2), as their x mu(2) supergroups do. The flags of the weight-1 groups stored in the database could not be checked here, and under the suggested text ZYa's example D_6 in O(2) (weight 0, not in the database) would not be maximal. The same generated pages contradict the previous sentence too ('we list only rational minimal supergroups'), for SU(2) x mu(2) and N(U(1)) x mu(2).
- `st_group.trace_zero_density` (Error or typo): The trace can be constant and nonzero on a component: for a finite Sato-Tate group such as μ(n) (0.1.n) every component is a point, where the trace is a root of unity. The ratio formula is unaffected, since such components contribute nothing to the probability. In odd weight the trace is zero on every component where it is constant (the Hodge circle passes through −1), so the corrected text keeps that true clause (round AO).
- `test.text` (Error or typo): The integral of x^(s-1) e^(-x) over (0, infinity) is Gamma(s), not Gamma(s) zeta(s); the formula behind the continuation is Gamma(s) zeta(s) = integral of x^(s-1)/(e^x - 1) for Re(s) > 1 (at s = 2 the two integrals are 1 and pi^2/6 = 1.6449..., computed). The knowl is a rendering test, so the formula is only sample text.

- `nf.is_galois` (Suggested category: ring): Defines a Galois extension for an arbitrary field extension via Aut(K/F) and its fixed field: general field theory, though Galois theory could instead be gathered in gg. Another possible category: `gg`. Confidence: medium.
- `nf.separable` (Suggested category: ring): Defines separable elements and separable extensions for an arbitrary finite field extension (general field theory); the remark that extensions of local and global fields are separable is only an application.
- `nf.separable_algebra` (Suggested category: ring): Defines finite separable (etale) algebras over an arbitrary field and their base change: general algebra, used by nf.local_algebra and the sibling and twin algebras but not specific to number fields.
- `nf.sibling` (Suggested category: gg): Defines sibling fields and algebras (non-isomorphic, with isomorphic Galois closures) over any ground field; `gg.other_representations` gives their group-theoretic side, although the number field pages display sibling fields. Another possible category: `nf`. Confidence: medium.
- `nf.stem_field` (Suggested category: gg): Stem fields of a Galois extension are the fields whose Galois closure it is, that is the fields attached to its transitive permutation representations, used by `gg.resolvents` and `artin.stem_field`; the definition itself is general field theory, so `ring` would fit as well. Another possible category: `ring`. Confidence: low.
- `nf.weil_polynomial` (Suggested category: av.fq): Weil q-polynomials and their relation to the characteristic polynomials of simple abelian varieties over 𝔽_q are Honda–Tate theory, like `av.fq.weil_polynomial`.
- `st_group.symplectic_form` (Suggested category: alg): A non-degenerate alternating bilinear form on a vector space over any field is linear algebra, like `alg.symmetric_bilinear_form`, `alg.matrix.skew_symmetric` and `alg.symplectic_isomorphism`.
